newsitem.title: USA: High water threatening rail lines in Minnesota.
newsitem.headline: High water threatening rail lines in Minnesota.

text.p: Railroad operations in the Dakotas and Minnesota were impeded Tuesday by high water with some rail lines south of Minneapolis-St.Paul possibly being closed later this week, railroad officials said.
Three railroads in the region said most of their main lines were open Tuesday, but some branch lines are closed.
Burlington Northern Santa Fe spokesman Jim Sabourin said, "We did reopen one of our two main tracks between Chicago and the Twin Cities Monday afternoon. The other line remained closed."
The reopened line may be closed again Wednesday if water continues to rise on the Mississippi River, he said. The threatened area lies southeast of the Twin Cities near the Wisconsin border.

As of late Monday, the Mississippi River at Minneapolis was at 16.1 feet and was expected to crest April 11 at 20 feet, four feet above the flood level. In LaCrosse, Wis, the river was 13.5 feet, 1.5 feet above flood level, and was seen cresting between April 12-15 at 16.5 feet. according to an Army Corps of Engineers spokeswoman.
Union Pacific Corp spokesman Ed Trandahl said none of the railroad's main lines were under water but some feeder lines were impassable.
"We have a lot of (Twin Cities' area) customers we can't serve right now because they are blocked off," he said.
Rising water on the Minnesota River may soon threaten Burlington Northern's line that serves Minneapolis, Savage and Mankato, Minn., he said.
The Minnesota River was 709.9 feet above sea level Tuesday morning, nearly 11 feet above the flood level, and was scheduled to crest April 14 at 716 feet, the Corps of Engineers said.
Grain elevators at Savage said they will be suspending operations this week because of high water on the Minnesota River was expected to cover roads and railroad tracks.

"We have some branch lines in the Dakotas that are closed because of water problems," said John Bergene, spokesman for Canadian Pacific LTD. "Our main line coming into the Twin Cities from the west are fine."
Waves from high water on the Mississippi River are threatening Canadian Pacific's track that extends from the Twin Cities to LaCross, Wis., he said.
